To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the optimal detection statistic for gravitational wave signals in non-Gaussian detector noise is a clipped version of the standard cross-correlation statistic, and that, for stochastic signals in non-Gaussain noise, the optimal detection statistic is a sum of a clipped cross-correlation term and an autocorrelation, or ‘‘self-noise,’’ term.

, when the noise is non-Gaussian, the optimal detection statistics are not the usual ones, but are instead the ones we have derived, and that the resulting detection probabilities can be computed using the Bayesian framework.

the signal detection techniques derived in ~paper I! for gravitational wave detectors are robust to non-Gaussian noise tails, that they can be derived in a Bayesian framework, and that they automatically eliminate the problematic autocorrelated term when applied to stochastic signals.
In summary, our research is concerned with
signal detection in non-Gaussian, non-stationary, non-white noise
the detection of signals in the presence of noise with non-Gaussian tails, and the present paper shows that the methods derived in paper I are also optimal from a Bayesian point of view.
the detection of weak signals in noise with non-Gaussian tails, and we have found a set of robust detection techniques which are near-optimal in both the frequentist and Bayesian frameworks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, in the limit considered here, the probability that the signal is present in data is to a very good approximation a monotomic function of the near-optimal signal detector derived in paper I, and that this probability can be computed from the data without the need to make any additional assumptions about the noise distribution.
the detection statistics derived in paper I are near-optimal, in a sense that can be made rigorous, for both deterministic signals and stochastic signals in noise whose tails are non-Gaussian.
the detection statistics derived in the previous paper are near-optimal in a wide range of situations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have derived optimal signal detection techniques in non-Gaussian detector noise for both deterministic and random signals.

, when the noise is non-Gaussian, the standard cross correlation statistic should be replaced by the generalized cross correlation statistic, which is obtained by truncating or discarding the non-Gaussian noise tails in the data before cross-correlating.
we have shown how to derive optimal signal detection techniques for non-Gaussian noise in both frequentist and Bayesian frameworks.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is not only possible, but in some cases necessary, to use non-Gaussian noise statistics in order to achieve the best possible performance for gravitational wave detection.
, for both deterministic signals and stochastic backgrounds of gravitational waves, the optimal detection statistic is to a good extent robust with respect to non-Gaussian tails in the noise.

, in the presence of non-Gaussian noise, the standard methods for signal detection, which have been used in gravitational wave astronomy since its inception ~e.g., the matched filter!, are not optimal, and that the optimal methods are simple to implement and can be used with existing data analysis software.
